about: The setup guide's shipped question set (STORY-atlas-setup-guide-adrs). Data, read by setup_guide.py; an install adds its own topics through ATLAS_SETUP_QUESTIONS_FILE without editing this file. Topic and question ids, and option values, are a CONTRACT: other parts of Atlas read answers by `<topic>.<question>` (the guardrail matrix, the first CI/CD flow), so a new meaning gets a new id or a new version of this file, never a reused one. setup_guide.py's header lists the keys.

topics.title: Guardrails for agents
topics.summary: What agents may do on their own, where a person must approve, and who merges and deploys.

questions.prompt: Which of these may an agent do without asking a person first?

options.label: read code, documents and the backlog
push a branch and open a pull request

questions.prompt: Which of these always need a person's explicit approval, whoever performs them?

options.label: changing a work item's acceptance criteria
adding, rotating or revoking a secret
changing who may see or do what

questions.prompt: Who merges a pull request?

options.label: an agent, after a person has approved it
an agent, once every required check is green

questions.prompt: Who deploys to production?

options.label: an agent, after a person has approved it
the pipeline, automatically after a merge

questions.prompt: Anything else an agent must never do, or must always ask about?

adr.title: Guardrails for agents
adr.context: Agents work in this organisation's repositories and services. Without a recorded rule, each agent decides for itself what it may do alone, and a person finds out afterwards.
adr.decision: Agents may do the following without asking: {agent_actions}. These always need a person's explicit approval: {approval_gates}. Who merges a pull request: {who_merges}. Who deploys to production: {who_deploys}. Further rules: {notes}.
adr.consequences: An agent asks before anything outside the allowed list, and stops at every approval gate even when it could technically continue. Changing these rules is a new answer in the setup guide, which records a new decision superseding this one.

topics.title: Continuous integration and delivery
topics.summary: Where checks run, which of them block a merge, and what starts a deploy.

questions.prompt: Where do automated checks run?
Which checks run on a change?
Which of those checks must pass before a change can merge?
What starts a deploy to production?

options.label: a person starts it by hand
a merge to the main branch

adr.title: Continuous integration and delivery
adr.context: Agents and people both change code here, and both need to know which checks judge a change and which of them can stop it.
adr.decision: Where checks run: {ci_platform}. The checks a change runs: {checks}. The checks that must pass before it merges: {gates}. What starts a production deploy: {deploy_trigger}.
adr.consequences: A change is not done until its gating checks are green, and a check that is not a gate is information, not a blocker. The first pipeline can be generated from these answers.

topics.title: Environments
topics.summary: The environments this organisation runs, by its own names.

questions.prompt: Which environments do you run? Give your own names, comma-separated, from the least to the most protected (for example: dev, test, prod).
Which of those names is production?
How does a change reach production?

options.label: each environment is deployed on its own

adr.title: Environments
adr.context: Rules about deploying and approving are written per environment, so the environments need names everyone, people and agents, uses the same way.
adr.decision: The environments are, from the least to the most protected: {names}. Production is {production}. How a change reaches production: {promotion}.
adr.consequences: Guardrails and pipelines name these environments and no others. Adding or renaming one is a new answer, which supersedes this decision.

topics.title: Identity and access
topics.summary: How people sign in, and whether access is decided per project.

questions.prompt: How do people sign in to Atlas?

options.label: the organisation's identity provider (OIDC single sign-on)
single sign-on, with local accounts kept for break-glass

questions.prompt: Should access be decided per project, with roles?

options.label: no: every signed-in person sees what is shared

questions.prompt: Is a new project visible to everyone, or only to the people given a role on it?

options.label: only to people with a role on it

adr.title: Identity and access
adr.context: Who can sign in, and what each person and their agents can see, has to be decided before people start working in Atlas.
adr.decision: How people sign in: {login}. Access per project: {rbac}. A new project is: {default_visibility}.
adr.consequences: The install's identity and access settings follow this decision; an agent acts with its person's access, never more. Changing it is a new answer, which supersedes this decision.

topics.title: Secrets handling
topics.summary: Where secrets live, and what an agent may do with them.

questions.prompt: Where are secrets kept?

options.label: files readable only by the service that needs them

questions.prompt: What may an agent do with a secret?

options.label: pass a secret's path to a tool, never read the value
read a secret scoped to its own task

questions.prompt: When are secrets rotated?

options.label: by hand, when someone decides to

adr.title: Secrets handling
adr.context: Agents run commands and write files, so a secret handled carelessly ends up in a log, a transcript or a repository.
adr.decision: Where secrets are kept: {storage}. What an agent may do with a secret: {agent_access}. When secrets are rotated: {rotation}.
adr.consequences: No secret is written into a repository, a command line, a work item or Atlas. Changing the rule is a new answer, which supersedes this decision.

topics.title: Work hierarchy
topics.summary: How work is broken down, and who files and judges it.

questions.prompt: How is work broken down?

options.label: epics contain stories, stories contain tasks

questions.prompt: Who files work items?
Who decides a work item's acceptance criteria?

options.label: an agent proposes them and a person approves

adr.title: Work hierarchy
adr.context: People and agents file work in the same backlog, so they need one way to break it down and one rule for who judges it.
adr.decision: How work is broken down: {levels}. Who files work items: {who_files}. Who decides acceptance criteria: {acceptance}.
adr.consequences: The board and the agents use this breakdown. Changing it is a new answer, which supersedes this decision.
